1Bayes’ theorem: partitions of the sample space

The board is headed Bayes' Theorem.

Definitionpartition of the sample space

Let and be a partition of the sample space .

( in the picture.)

Explanation (added)

A partition asks for two things at once. The pieces are mutually exclusive (no outcome is in two of them, ) and exhaustive (together they are all of ). Put together: every outcome is in exactly one .

The smallest partition you already know is and (): Lecture 4's complement rule is the statement that the two pieces of that partition use up all the probability.

Textbook Devore §2.4, p. 80. The book does not use the word “partition”; it says the events are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, and it uses where the board uses . Figure 2.11 (p. 80) is this picture drawn with four pieces.

If is an event in the sample space , then the partition of can be used to construct a partition of .

Why the pieces of are disjoint. An outcome in would have to be in both and , and no outcome is. Why they cover . Any outcome in is in , so it is in exactly one , so it is in exactly one .

Why the union becomes a sum. That is the third probability axiom from Lecture 3: for disjoint events, the probability of the union is the sum of the probabilities. If you are asked to justify this line, “the events are mutually exclusive, so the probabilities add” is the sentence to write.

and want to find for some .  ↖ (posterior probability)

How do we find ?

Explanation (added)

Prior means before we know whether happened; posterior means after we are told it did. The information we are given runs “forward” (given the piece , how likely is ?), and the question runs “backward” (given , how likely is the piece ?). Bayes' theorem is the rule for turning one into the other.

In general and are different numbers. In the calculator example below, but .

Textbook The words prior and posterior are introduced with Example 2.29, p. 80, and used in the statement of Bayes' theorem, p. 81.
TheoremBayes' theorem

(The first photo shows only the first line, with the “disjoint union” lines from the previous board still below it. The second photo has the last line added.)

Explanation (added)

Three steps, each one a rule you already have:

1. is the definition of conditional probability (Lectures 5 and 6).
2. The denominator is replaced by the sum over the partition from the previous board.
3. Every , top and bottom, is rewritten with the multiplication rule , because those are the numbers we are actually given.

Notice the numerator is one of the terms of the denominator. So the answer is always “this piece's share of ”: a number between 0 and 1, and the posteriors add to 1.

Textbook Bayes' Theorem, equation (2.6), p. 81. Devore writes each product in the other order, , uses for the piece of interest and requires .

2Bayes’ theorem with a tree diagram

We can also do this using a tree diagram.

Let's just consider the case for this (easy extension) and find .

(On the board the numerator is in blue and the denominator in black, and the fraction runs across two board panels.)

Explanation (added)

The tree is the formula laid out as a picture, so you do not have to memorise the formula:

1. Multiply along a path to get the probability at its leaf (multiplication rule, Lecture 6).
2. Add the leaves that end in to get .
3. Divide the leaf you care about by that total.

The leaves are never used for . They are there because the two branches out of each must add to 1: .

In the first photo the left edge is cut off (“[W]e can also…”, “[Let']s just consider…”) and the first path product is partly hidden by the instructor's arm; the second photo shows all of it.

Textbook p. 81, just after (2.6): with only a few events in the partition, a tree diagram can be used to get posterior probabilities without referring to Bayes' theorem explicitly. The book draws its trees left to right (Figure 2.10, p. 79; Figure 2.12, p. 82); the board draws them top to bottom.

3Example: the defective calculator

Exampledefective calculators

You run a store that sells calculators.

60% of your calculators come from company A, 30% come from company B, and the remaining 10% come from company C.

You have noticed that 2% of the calculators from company A are defective, 5% from company B are defective, and 10% of the calculators from company C are defective.

An employee randomly selects a calculator from your store and finds that [it] is defective. He tells you he found a defective calculator but does not show it to you.

(On the board “calculators” is misspelled once as “calcutors”, and the word “it” is missing from “finds that is defective”.)

Explanation (added)

Match the story to the theory before computing anything. The three companies are the partition: every calculator comes from exactly one of them. “Defective” is the event of the theory (called here). The 60%, 30%, 10% are the priors; the 2%, 5%, 10% are the conditional probabilities ; and “he found a defective one” is the information we condition on.

What is the probability the calculator comes from company A?

4Random variables

The board is headed Random Variables  (rv).

Definitionrandom variable

A random variable is a function with domain equal to the sample space of an experiment.

A random variable is a function that assigns a value to each outcome in the sample space.

Explanation (added)

The two sentences say the same thing. A function needs inputs and outputs: the inputs are the outcomes of the experiment (the domain is ) and the outputs are numbers. Nothing about itself is random. The randomness is in which outcome the experiment produces; then reports a number for it.

Notation to get used to: a capital letter () is the random variable, the rule. A lower-case letter (, or on the board) is one particular value it can give.

Textbook Devore §3.1, definition on p. 96: a random variable is “any rule that associates a number with each outcome in ”, a function whose domain is the sample space and whose range is the set of real numbers. The book writes for “ is the value gives to the outcome ”.
Examplethree fair coins

We are going to run a simple experiment where we flip 3 fair coins.

The random variable will assign a value to the outcome that is equal to the number of heads we get (let count the number of heads).

Outcomes:   TTT,   TTH, THT, HTT,   THH, HTH, HHT,   HHH.

Explanation (added)

This is the same sample space as Lecture 4's three coins: 8 equally likely outcomes. sorts them into groups by number of heads, and the group sizes are (they add to 8). Those sizes are the combinations from Lecture 5: there are ways to choose which of the 3 flips are heads, so , , , .

The payoff of a random variable is shorter language. Instead of the event we can write “”.

Textbook Compare Exercise 1 of §3.1 (p. 98), which is this example with beams in place of coins. Examples 3.1–3.3 (pp. 96–97) define random variables in the same way, by saying what number goes with each outcome.

5Discrete and continuous random variables

The board is headed Definitions.

Definitiondiscrete random variable

A discrete random variable is a random variable whose range is a finite set or a countably infinite set.

(The range of in the example is the set . This random variable is a discrete random variable.)

Definitioncontinuous random variable

A continuous random variable is a random variable whose range can be written [as] a disjoint union of intervals and the probability that the random variable assigns any [valu]e in its range is 0.

(The three photos show this board being built up. In the last one the left ends of the final two lines are blocked by a person; the bracketed letters are supplied, and they agree with the book's wording.)

Explanation (added)

Countably infinite means the values can be listed in order, a first, a second, a third and so on, even though the list never ends: is the standard example, and it is exactly the range in the “flip until the first head” example later in this lecture. Counts are discrete.

A continuous random variable measures rather than counts (a time, a length, a voltage). Its range is an interval such as , and the second half of the definition says every single value has probability 0: . Probability then comes from intervals of values, which is Chapter 4. Everything else today is about discrete random variables.

Textbook p. 98, “Two Types of Random Variables”. The discrete definition matches the board (“finite … or countably infinite”). The continuous definition is given as two numbered conditions: the possible values are an interval or a disjoint union of intervals, and for every possible value .

Last example:

(The first photo was taken before the “Last example” line was written. Glare covers the start of the word “provided”. The third subscript in the bracketed example reads as a 7.)

Explanation (added)

These are the three probability axioms from Lectures 3 and 4, restated for the events “”.

① Every probability is between 0 and 1.
② gives each outcome only one value, so the events “” for different values cannot happen together. They are disjoint, so their probabilities add. In words: the probability that lands in a set of values is the sum of over that set. For the coins, .
③ Every outcome gets some value, so the events “” form a partition of , the same idea as at the start of this lecture. Adding over all of them gives .

How this gets used: to decide whether a table can be a pmf, check ① and ③. To find a missing entry or an unknown constant, set the total equal to 1 and solve.

Textbook p. 100, right after the definition: the conditions and “are required of any pmf”. The book does not list ② as a separate condition; it simply uses it, as in Example 3.7 (p. 100) where .

Explanation (added)

Because makes sense for any real number , the graph is defined everywhere, and it is a step function:

• For , no value of is , so . That is the heavy line along the negative -axis ending in an open dot at 0.
• Between two values nothing new is added, so the graph is flat. For example .
• At each value of the graph jumps up by . The filled dot is on the upper step because “” includes the value itself: , not .
• Once everything has been added, so from there on.

So never decreases, starts at 0 on the far left and ends at 1 on the far right. Written out piecewise:

Textbook examples worth reading

Example 2.29 (pp. 78–80). Three brands of DVD player with different shares of sales and different warranty-repair rates. Three questions in a row: a joint probability, the overall repair rate, and the posterior for each brand. It is the calculator example with other numbers and a tree.

Example 2.31 (pp. 81–82). A test for a disease that 1 adult in 1000 has. The test is right 99% of the time on people with the disease and 98% of the time on people without it, yet a positive result means only about a 4.7% chance of disease, because the people without it vastly outnumber the people with it. A good one for seeing how much the prior matters.

Example 3.10 (pp. 101–102). Five blood donors, two of whom have the type being looked for, are tested in random order until one is found. The pmf is built with the multiplication rule for sampling without replacement (Lecture 6), then put in a table and a line graph.

Example 3.13 (pp. 104–105). A cdf for a random variable whose values are not consecutive (1, 2, 4, 8, 16). It shows at numbers that are not possible values, writes piecewise and graphs the steps.

Example 3.14 (pp. 105–106). The cdf for “number of births until the first boy”: today's first-head example with a general .

What a typical exam question looks like

• A Bayes question with three sources. You are given what share comes from each source and a rate for each source (defective, late, positive test). Find the probability that an item with the property came from a named source. Expected work: name the events, draw the tree, multiply along the paths, add for the denominator, divide.

• The overall rate on its own: “what is the probability a randomly chosen item is defective?” That is only the denominator, .
